name: Rhapontic rhubarb root extract (Rheum rhaponticum)
short: German postmarketing: 124 adverse-event reports, mostly allergic reactions (74) and gut symptoms (47). Trial: 11 events in 5 women on extract vs 3 in 3 on placebo; endometrial biopsies did not differ.
text: These sources concern one standardised root extract of Rheum rhaponticum (rhapontic rhubarb) taken by mouth by women with menopausal symptoms; they do not apply to other rhubarb species. Postmarketing reports: from 1993 to June 2014, about 140 million daily doses were placed on the German market and 124 adverse-event reports were recorded, most commonly hypersensitivity (74 reactions) and gastrointestinal symptoms (47 reactions); in North America, 79 consumer complaints of a physical response were recorded from January 2009 to June 2014 (about 13 million tablets sold), mainly gastrointestinal symptoms (23) and failure to work (22). These are spontaneous reports, which cannot show how often harms occur or prove cause. Trials: in a 12-week placebo-controlled trial in 109 perimenopausal women, there were no differences between the groups in gynaecological findings, including endometrial biopsies and bleeding, or in weight, blood pressure, pulse and laboratory safety values, and no adverse events were classified as related to the extract. Women from that trial continued in two 48-week observational phases (51 in the second), with no clinically relevant change in safety parameters and no adverse events observed in relation to long-term use. In a second 12-week placebo-controlled trial in 112 perimenopausal women, 14 adverse events were reported: 11 by 5 women taking the extract and 3 by 3 women taking placebo. In a 6-month observational study that enrolled 363 women at 70 German gynaecology practices (results after 6 months are given for 252), one adverse event was reported and assessed as unrelated. Breast cancer (observational): in a German prescription database study, the 5,686 women prescribed the extract had no higher odds of a breast cancer diagnosis than 17,058 matched women without it (odds ratio 1.01, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.26), and 2,616 of them had no higher odds than 7,848 women prescribed hormone therapy (odds ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.69 to 1.33); this is an association study, and the abstract does not say how long the women took it. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
